pages.text:
Background
Much of the research conducted for this project was focused on key design changes to last year’s
vessel. The hull was kept the same from last year’s vessel due to the reasoning that the 2026
team seeks to maximize velocity, and a V-shaped hull can perform at higher velocities compared
to a catamaran. Although the V-shape sacrifices stability compared to a catamaran, the 2026
team considered the tradeoff and made the final decision to try and reach higher speeds. The
lightweight fiberglass hull paired with the V-shape should allow the boat to cut water effectively
by reducing the wetted surface area of the hull, which in turn lowers skin friction and wave
making resistance. A recent UB alumnus, Jake DeFrancisco, helped fabricate the fiberglass hull
for the 2025 boat and gave the 2026 team a list of design changes the 2025 team would like to
have incorporated to improve the design. From that list, the 2026 team decided to significantly
alter propeller design, integrate a water-cooling system, and introduce cavitation cylinders.
The 2026 team is using two 475kV Leopard 5692 brushless motors, one which rotates clockwise
and the other which rotates counterclockwise to ensure that the propellers are counterrotating.
Eight LiPo batteries power the vessel ensuring that the propulsion is electric, and a Futaba
receiver is used to control the two Leopard motors as well as a servo motor that controls the
rudder.
The first major design change for the boat is a completely new propeller design. While the 2025
team had two-blade stock propellers made of a beryllium alloy, the 2026 team modeled over ten
three-blade propellers in SolidWorks. Four variations were chosen for fabrication due to the
varying pitch, tip diameter, and hub thickness. The variations were additively manufactured by
Moog under the supervision of John Renaldo, the Engineering Design Lead at Moog Space and
Defense Group. Thanks to John, the 2026 team was able to print the propeller variations out of
316L stainless steel as well as a PAHT-CF material. Both the 316L and PAHT-CF are corrosionresistant, which is optimal for marine applications.
The next major design change is the integration of a water-cooling system. The 2025 had
architecture for a water-cooling system already partially installed but was unable to get the water
to enter the two pickups drilled in the rudder. Temperature sensors in the ESC monitor
temperature with tubing running through the inside of the hull and connecting to inlets on the
motors and speed controllers and exiting on two outlets on the side of the hull.
Lastly, the 2026 team aimed to reduce cavitation. The 2025 team had two plates placed above the
propellers to try and reduce cavitation, but the 2026 team included cavitation cylinders.
Cavitation around the propellers of a vessel can significantly decrease efficiency by reducing
thrust and disrupting flow.

content. The high tensile strength measured for the six-layer fiberglass hull (19,260.75 ±
1,439.31 lb/in²) gave our team confidence that the hull would remain structurally sound under
expected loading conditions.
The previous team also tested the boat with an additional 30 lb. load, which conveniently aligns
with this year’s updated competition requirement. Under two 30 lb. payloads, the measured draft
was only 3.2 inches below the waterline. Since this represents less than one-third of the boat’s
total depth, our team considered the result practical for operation. Additional testing is planned
with varied payload placement to ensure the stern sits slightly deeper than the bow, rather than
maintaining a fully level position, which may improve stability and performance.

Water-Cooling System
The water-cooling system was chosen to be implemented since the 2024-2025 and 2023-2024
team both had overheating problems within their boat. The 2024-2025 team had set up the watercooling system but did not get the system to run. After looking at their system, the team
concluded that there was not enough pressure for the water to flow through the system. The team
has redesigned the system to include more inlet locations and redid the architecture of the tubing
to increase the pressure flowing into the system.
The inner diameter of the tubing was already decided by the 2024-2025 team, which was
selected as 4.5 mm. The inlet for the tubing needed to have a bigger diameter, so the team
decided to find how the pressure loss would affect the flow in the tubing. The tubing at the inlets
starts at 6 mm and decreases to 4.5 mm. The inlet was chosen based on the current holes cut into
the boat from the propellers. The holes for the propeller system needed to be replaced to allow
for higher velocity. The inlets chosen are shown in figure 2 below.

Cavitation Cylinders
Cavitation cylinders are used to reduce cavitation, which occurs when bubbles from propeller
turbulence collapse and cause damage and efficiency loss. Positioned closely around the
propellers, they help direct water flow more smoothly through the system. The cylinders remain
stationary as part of the propeller strut, working with the rotating propellers to improve overall
performance and durability.
In Figure 7 you can see the nozzle prototype design. The nozzle was designed with a cylindrical
throat, and gentle tapered outlet to improve water flow through the propeller and increase thrust at
low speed. This geometry is preferred over a simple cylinder because it guides and accelerates the
incoming water smoothly, reduces losses, and improves efficiency for a heavily loaded smalldiameter propeller. A constant wall thickness in PETG was selected to provide structural strength,
print reliability, and resistance to vibration and water exposure during operation. This design is
commonly used on heavily loaded propellers such as those on tugboats and trawlers where
increased thrust is required. Because the hull is relatively small and lightweight compared with the
60-pound payload, the propulsion system must generate high thrust from a small 2.5-inch diameter
propeller, creating operating conditions similar to those of a tugboat where a relatively small
propeller must move a large load at low speed. This makes a ducted nozzle appropriate because,
in proportional terms, the boat behaves like a heavily loaded low speed vessel, where thrust
enhancement and reduction of losses are more important.

Overview of Build & Fabrication Processes
Power Storage
The power storage system is made up of a configuration of eight 14.8 Volt, 4s 5200 mAh lithium
polymer batteries. The power is stored in these eight batteries and connected to a kill switch that
controls the flow of power from the batteries to its associated electrical components. The
batteries power the motor, the telemetry sensor, two electronic speed controllers, the bilge pump,
the servo and receiver. The full system uses 34V of power, well below the 55V max. This is
accomplished by connecting the batteries in both series and parallel, as shown in the diagram,
Figure 8, below. The electronics are soldered together with an 8-gauge wire and then
waterproofed by being wrapped in electrical tape. The telemetry sensor and the electronic speed
controller (ESC) are remotely controlled by the Futaba 4PM Plus RC Controller and Receiver.
The remote controller has an effective operating range of about 230 feet (70 meters) under
optimal conditions. The power flows out of the batteries and into these components, while the
remote controller uses the servo to steer the vessel and the motors to control the amount of
power/speed being translated from the motors, down the drive shafts, to the propellers that is
thrusting the vessel forward.

The power storage system is unique due to the configuration of the batteries in parallel and
series. The batteries are configured as seen in Figure 8 because it allows the batteries, which
have a higher voltage capability, to perform within the competition requirements. Configuring
the batteries to preform within the competition requirements was done through both research and
testing. By using a multimeter set to DC Voltage and connecting the positive probe to the
positive terminal, and the negative probe to the negative terminal, the voltage was observed on
the display screen of the multimeter. Additionally, it was observed that while the configuration
maintains a system output of 34V while the batteries are held at 4.2V per cell, the system
decreases to 31V when the batteries are held at 3.8V per cell.

year’s boat. The driveshafts, drive dogs, propellers and bullet collars were all improved upon.

propelling the boat forward. The propellers operate by rotating with the drive shaft, powered by

Powertrain
The powertrain system was mostly replaced and improved upon this year from the previous
year’s boat. The driveshafts, drive dogs, propellers and bullet collars were all improved upon.
The propeller is additively manufactured from CRES 316L Stainless Steel through MOOG from
SolidWorks designs made by the team. The propeller is different in both material and
configuration. While the previous propellers had two blades, the new propellers have three
blades and a larger diameter, which provides more surface area for displacing the water and
propelling the boat forward. The propellers operate by rotating with the drive shaft, powered by
the motor it is connected to. The propellers are secured in between the drive dog and bullet
collar. There are two propellers alongside each other, each rotating opposite directions. They
rotate towards each other to balance out torque and cancel out side-force, which can also be
referred to as “prop-walk”. This allows the vessel to travel straight without excessive steering
correction. If the propellers rotated in the same direction, the vessel would travel in a circle
without steering correction, and steering correction would be very difficult.

The propeller is kept on the shaft by being placed in between a drive dog and a bullet collar. The
drive dog acts as a base against the thrust washer. The drive dog has pawls which fit into the
notches on the propeller as an interlocking method. Then the thrust washer, drive dog, and
propeller are kept on the shaft by the bullet collar at the end of the shaft. The bullet collar is

pages.text:
placed on at the end of the configuration and has a set screw which holds it on the shaft. THe
bullet collar then keeps the other components on and is tapered to a tip, similar to the shape of a
bullet, for hydrodynamic purposes.
The propellers were designed to fit on the stock shaft, in between the thrust washer, drive dog,
and bullet collar. It was important to ensure the dimensions of the custom designed propeller
could fit properly with the rest of the stock components. If the dimensions for the length of the
propeller or the inner and outer diameter were incorrect, it could result in manufacturing a
propeller which does not fit with the rest of the system. This would be a very bad situation that
could result in a failed project. With the propeller’s dimensions correct, it is designed to interact
and function cohesively within the system.
From the drive shaft, where the propeller, drive dog, thrust washer, and bullet collar are secured,
the drive shaft is then connected into the motors. The motors convert the electrical energy from
the batteries into the driveshafts which spin and translates the power into the propellers which
give the boat thrust, which is called propulsion. The motors themselves convert the electrical
power into mechanical rotational energy, which is controlled by the remote controller, an
electronic speed controller (ESC) which manages speed and torque, as well as direction. The
direction is controlled through the same remote control, but it is connected to a servo motor that
controls the rudder.

Controls
The vessel’s control system consists of an electronic speed controller (ESC), steering servo,
transmitter and receiver that has been optimized by the PEP26 team. Two Hydro XLX2 ESCs are
used (one for each motor), providing independent motor control and enhanced maneuverability.
These ESCs feature an integrated water-cooling system, which was incorporated into the boat’s
system to maintain safe operating temperature and also transmits real-time temperature data to
the controller for performance monitoring. Steering is achieved using a Theta THL398 servo to
ensure precise and responsive control under varying conditions. The controller is a Futaba 4Pm
Plus transmitter paired with an R304SB-E receiver, which uses high speed signal processing and
built in telemetry to improve response time.

Propulsion
Propeller
The propellers are a key component in the propulsion system. Connected to the powertrain, the
motors provide rotational power through the drive shafts to the propellers. The propellers, one
forward and the other mirrored to be reversed, correlate with the forward and reversed drive
shafts. Forward and reversed denote the rotational direction of the shafts and propellers. One
rotates clockwise, while the other rotates counterclockwise. This opposing rotation, that each
rotate towards each other, allow the boat to drive straight without steering correction. In the case
where the propellers are configured differently, rotating in the same direction, it would cause the
boat to turn in a circle and create difficulty in steering.

The propellers were designed to fit on the stock shaft, in between the thrust washer, drive dog,
and bullet collar. It was important to ensure the dimensions of the custom designed propeller
could fit properly with the rest of the stock components. If the dimensions for the length of the
propeller or the inner and outer diameter were incorrect, it could result in manufacturing a
propeller which does not fit with the rest of the system. This would be a very bad situation that
could result in a failed project. With the propeller’s dimensions correct, it is designed to interact
and function cohesively within the system.

From the drive shaft, where the propeller, drive dog, thrust washer, and bullet collar are secured,
the drive shaft is then connected into the motors. The motors convert the electrical energy from
the batteries into the driveshafts which spin and translates the power into the propellers which
give the boat thrust, which is called propulsion. The motors themselves convert the electrical
power into mechanical rotational energy, which is controlled by the remote controller, an
electronic speed controller (ESC) which manages speed and torque, as well as direction. The
direction is controlled through the same remote control, but it is connected to a servo motor that
controls the rudder.

The propellers were tested in the water, attached to the drive shafts with the drive dogs and bullet
collars securing them in place. The PAHT-CF clockwise propellers, as shown above in Figure 9,
were compared to the CRES 316L propellers. The PAHT-CF propellers required annealing after
they were additively manufactured in order to increase the crystallinity which in turn increases
the strength. This allows them to perform reliably alongside the metal propellers during testing.

Water-Cooling
Before materials were ordered and in-water testing began, an Arduino prototype was developed
to simulate the thermal conditions within the system. This prototype consisted of three DHT11
temperature and humidity sensors used to represent the thermal behavior of the three motors. An
LCD screen was integrated to display real-time temperature data, allowing the team to monitor
system response under simulated overheating conditions (Figure 10).

This initial prototype also included a pump activation, where water flow would be triggered once
a percentage of the temperature threshold was exceeded. While this validated the feasibility of
active cooling, it introduced more complexity to the system and increased power requirements.
So, the design was iterated toward a simpler passive cooling approach.
The PEP25 team experienced issues with the rudder-based water pickup system, likely due to
partial blockage of the inlet and insufficient pressure to drive water through the system. The
PEP26 design replaces the single rudder inlet with an inlet configuration that is positioned
behind the propellers. This placement takes advantage of the increased velocity generated by the
rotation of the propellers, improving the ability of water to enter and circulate through the
cooling system.

In addition to the cooling system, a separate bilge pump system was fabricated to manage any
water that enters the hull. The pump is a 6-12V pump that is running at 12V. The current usage
of the pump ends up being negligible compared to what is needed for the motors and rest of the
propulsion system so the bilge pump can come from the original 8 LiPo batteries but utilize a
DC-to-DC converter to step down the voltage and current. This also required an additional thru
hull fitting drilled into the side of the boat and dedicated tubing independent of the water-cooling
system. The bilge pump is mounted at the lowest point in the hull to maximize the efficiency and
is fastened to prevent movement during operation. The channel layout is shown below in Figure

Risk
The risks mitigated during the design and build include basic safety precautions when using
power tools and machines, like using safety glasses and ensuring hair is tied back and out of the
way. Additional steps include ensuring there are no strings or loose clothing around the
machines, as they could be caught in the machine or tool and pull the operator into the blade, bit,
tool, or machine in general. Safety is a top priority for the team and is taken very seriously.
There is no horseplay in the machine shops or around the boat. All things being operated upon
are discussed, measured, and drawn out before tools and machines are used so there is certainty
around the tools and machines. This step is taken because uncertainty around a power tool or
machine can lead to quick accidents and have the potential to place the operator in a dangerous
situation.
Another step taken to mitigate risks during the design and build process includes a type of buddy
system. No work has been done on the vessel using tools or machines without the
accompaniment of at least one other person. Having two people present when power tools and
machines are being used ensures that there is a second set of eyes to ensure that everything is
clamped properly, safety shields are in place, and all safety measures are being respected.
Having the buddy system also allows for a worst-case scenario emergency action plan. In a

Another step taken to mitigate risks during the design and build process includes a type of buddy

Having the buddy system also allows for a worst-case scenario emergency action plan. In a

pages.text:
worst-case scenario if an accident were to occur, and a team member becomes injured during the
design and build phase, the secondary person can call emergency services, EMS, and assist the
injured person with applying pressure to the injury, with the gloves kept next to the first aid kit in
the machine shop where all work is completed on the vessel. Multiple team members have basic
first aid certifications but that is not something relied upon and any and all injuries are to be
reported to emergency personnel, the machine shop advisor and the project advisor, Dr. Rashidi.
While no team members have been injured during the design and build process of this project, it
is important to have both a safety and emergency action plan to both mitigate risk and have a
structured plan for a worst-case scenario.
The risks that will be controlled during the race include overheating prevention through the
internal temperature sensors and incorporated water-cooling system as well as cavitation
cylinders around the propellers which will help prevent any accidental injuries from the propeller
blades. The inclusion of the kill switch, which will manually cut power to the motors is included
not only as a competition requirement, but for the safety of the crew and competitors.
Additionally, basic safety precautions will be taken, like wearing safety glasses when working on
the vessel, hair tied back and out of the way, as well as close-toed shoes and dry clothing. All
team members are required to read the PEP26 Safety Communication document prior to the
competition in an effort to ensure all members are on the same page for safety rules, are
informed on all safety protocols, the systems in place during the competition, and the
expectations.
Another way to mitigate and control risks during the race include refraining from operating on
the electronics while the vessel is in the water. While the electronics system is properly
insulated and waterproofed, to avoid any potential accidents, the electronics will not be changed
or worked on while the boat is in the water. In the instance where the electronics need to be
operated upon, the boat will be removed from the water, the kill switch will be taken out and the
internals of the boat will be dried with a dry towel, even if it does not appear to be wet, before
being touched. Additionally, the team members working on the electronics will be dry and have
dry hands. These steps are taken to avoid potential electrocution and mitigate the risks
associated with electronics in wet environments.
